source_refs.note: Book p. 4-5: 1.3 introduction, (i) Algebraic Functions (definition, examples), (ii) Transcendental Functions (definition, examples)

blocks.text: Algebraic and transcendental functions are the two basic classes of functions studied in mathematics. Together they play a vital role in modelling and understanding many real-world phenomena. In this section the focus is on the fundamental transcendental functions, namely the exponential and logarithmic functions.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Almost every function you used in Class XI (polynomials such as \(x^{2} - 5x + 6\), rational functions such as \(\frac{1}{x-2}\), roots such as \(\sqrt{x}\)) is built from \(x\) with ordinary algebra. Functions such as \(e^{x}\), \(\ln x\) and \(\sin x\) cannot be built that way: they "go beyond" algebra, which is what the word transcendental means. This section gives the precise dividing line between the two classes, because the rest of the unit studies the transcendental ones (exponential, logarithmic and hyperbolic functions).

A function \(y = f(x)\) is algebraic if it satisfies a polynomial equation of the form
\[P_{n}(x)y^{n} + P_{n-1}(x)y^{n-1} + \cdots\]
\[\quad + P_{1}(x)y + P_{0}(x) = 0\]
where each \(P_{i}(x)\) is a polynomial in \(x\) for \(i = 0, 1, 2, \ldots, n\) and atleast one \(P_{i}(x)\) is not identically zero for \(i = 1, 2, 3, \ldots, n\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints "atleast" as one word; the correct spelling is "at least". The mathematics of the definition is unchanged.

In simple words, a function \(y = f(x)\) is algebraic if it is obtained from \(x\) using a finite number of algebraic operations such as addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and \(n^{\text{th}}\) roots.
\(f(x) = 2x^{2} - 3x\), \(g(x) = \frac{x^{2}+1}{x-3},\ x \ne 3\), \(h(x) = (x+1)^{3/2}\) and \(k(x) = \sqrt{x+1}\) are examples of algebraic functions.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
How do these four satisfy the polynomial equation? Write \(y\) for the function and clear roots and fractions:
\(f\): \(y - (2x^{2} - 3x) = 0\) (here \(n = 1\), \(P_{1}(x) = 1\), \(P_{0}(x) = -(2x^{2} - 3x)\)).
\(g\): multiply by \(x - 3\): \((x - 3)y - (x^{2} + 1) = 0\).
\(h\): square both sides: \(y^{2} - (x + 1)^{3} = 0\).
\(k\): square both sides: \(y^{2} - (x + 1) = 0\).
Each is a polynomial equation in \(y\) whose coefficients are polynomials in \(x\). So roots and fractions do not make a function transcendental.
A function is called a transcendental function if it is not algebraic.
\(y = e^{x}\), \(y = 2^{x}\), \(y = \ln x\), \(y = \sin x\), \(y = \sin^{-1} x\), \(y = \sin x + \ln x\), \(y = e^{x^{2}}\) are examples of transcendental functions.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
In each of these, \(x\) sits inside an exponent, a logarithm or a trigonometric (or inverse trigonometric) function. No finite chain of \(+, -, \times, \div\) and roots produces them, and no polynomial equation in \(y\) is satisfied by them. (The full proof that, for example, \(e^{x}\) is not algebraic is beyond this level; we accept it.)
A quick sign: \(x^{2}\) is algebraic (the variable is the base), but \(2^{x}\) is transcendental (the variable is the exponent).

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: To classify a function, look for \(x\) inside an exponent, a \(\log\)/\(\ln\), or a trigonometric or inverse trigonometric function. If you find one (and it does not cancel out), the function is transcendental; otherwise it is algebraic. Then justify an algebraic answer by writing its polynomial equation, as in the teaching note above.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Algebraic: obtained from \(x\) by finitely many \(+, -, \times, \div\) and \(n^{\text{th}}\) roots; it satisfies a polynomial equation in \(y\).
2. Transcendental: any function that is not algebraic, e.g. \(e^{x}\), \(2^{x}\), \(\ln x\), \(\sin x\), \(\sin^{-1} x\).
3. Roots and fractions keep a function algebraic: \(\sqrt{x+1}\), \((x+1)^{3/2}\), \(\frac{x^{2}+1}{x-3}\).
4. A sum such as \(\sin x + \ln x\) or a composition such as \(e^{x^{2}}\) of transcendental functions is transcendental.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Calling \(\sqrt{x+1}\) or \((x+1)^{3/2}\) transcendental because of the root or the fractional power: roots are algebraic operations.
2. Calling \(2^{x}\) algebraic "because 2 is just a number": the variable is in the exponent, so it is transcendental. Do not confuse \(x^{2}\) with \(2^{x}\).
3. Forgetting the restriction \(x \ne 3\) for \(g(x) = \frac{x^{2}+1}{x-3}\): a rational function is undefined where its denominator is zero.
